title: community as creative practice
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

I love making art in the void, and I've felt called to build a community. this calling is probably precisely because I have such a complicated relationship with community. I've run away from them. I've chosen self-exile. I've swung from hyper-independence to over-responsibility.

in this episode, I'll share how I'm thinking of shaping my community as creative companionship, bounded by shared questing. I'll explore my four guiding values for a community -- like caring for a garden, weaving a dream catcher, or making an infinite feast. A community can be a living creative practice that feeds our inner worlds.

Hi friends, this is Botanical Studies of Internet Magic, a podcast on the alchemy of creative power through the vessel and portal of the internet. My name is Kening, and I'll be your guide.

This episode starts with a confession that even though I'm currently in the process of beginning the second season of my creative community, Labyrinth Library, I've always had a very complicated, ambivalent relationship to community. I wanna share a little bit about my personal story around community and feelings of non-belonging, unpack the cycle of ghosting and over-giving, and articulate my vision of what a creative community actually is as a group of people, creative friends bounded by shared questing, and then share with you my four guidelines or values for being part of and cultivating a community that is resilient, community as garden, as ecosystem, as shared world, which can feed itself over time.

the hermit

If you've been following my work for a while, you know that one of my core ethos is about making and sharing your work into the void. I have very much embraced the Hermit identity, the sense that I don't need the other to give me any kind of reaction or validation in order to keep doing this work. And the story that I told myself is that I don't need accountability or structure or support from anything external to keep doing hard things, that I have the fortitude and endurance through years, a decade of the lonely work.

All of that is true. I still am deeply anchored in the belief that whatever you create and share must first and foremost be for you rather than the reactions of the other. At the same time, when it comes to the ways in which we might resist or struggle with community at times does come from deeper emotional layers. And in my case, early feelings around non-belonging or feeling misunderstood.

the wounding

My resistance to community in my upbringing comes from growing up as a Chinese American immigrant child that being in community meant I had to conform and lose myself, lose parts of myself I was just discovering. Or it meant feeling like an outsider in the larger community of Southern small town America.

And I think even after I moved to New York City and joined artistic groups or writing groups or entrepreneurship groups or other creative artsy people, I realized that just because we were interested in the same things, that we were technically doing the same things, it didn't mean that we actually understood each other. The what was similar, but the why and the how were so very different.

And so because I struggled to find a community that I could really belong to, I always equated it with either limitation, like having a community would restrict my creative potential and smooth out my rough edges and force me to conform. Or I equated a community to loneliness and disappointment and pain because I believe that no community could truly see me or understand me, let alone support and resource my journey.

The story was that in order to find my truth and happiness, I must be alone and lonely. This sounds like self-inflicted torture because looking back now, I'm sure that perhaps it was just that I didn't look hard enough for the right communities. This kind of self-imposed exile was the path that I needed to walk. In order to eventually dismantle the false binary nature of being true to oneself and being in community with others.

Three years before starting Labyrinth, I wrote about it in a post, "A Hermit Growing Creative Community."

the ghosting cycle

And part of the struggle was that even when I started teaching creative classes and leading small circles in early 2020, I had moved too quickly from the hermit lifestyle to being in deep relationship with others, that I trapped myself into these unsustainable cycles.

I gave everyone there all of my creative energy, all of my sensitivity, the people, my students who arrived were beautiful people navigating big messy questions around their creative practices and their place in the world and their emotions. It was also during the pandemic. I went from avoiding being a part of other people's communities to holding space for my own such that I think everyone there took up residence in my head.

It was so easy for me to take on their struggles and burdens and to feel responsible for whether or not they had a good experience or were learning the course materials. And it was a deeply nourishing experience. It laid the foundation for everything that I've done since, but emotionally it was also very taxing.

I would fall into these cycles of giving everything very intensely, burning out and then disappearing, hiding, going back into my cave, exhausted.

Sometime in 2022, I stopped doing live creative classes altogether and just focused on web design clients.

the return

When I decided that I wanted to start again only a year ago, it was after years of feeling this intuition that there's something in my creative destiny, shall we say, that felt like it was meant to lead a community, that the fact that I was a hermit for so long and that my work is very specific means that the people who are drawn to it are deeply sensitive, empathic, creative, intuitive people and that something magical could happen if we all gather together.

In this past year, each time I gathered people for a live experience, I would ask myself, how can I structure this? How can I design this container such that it would nourish me instead of depleting me? And how can I do this for a longer communal container that is not one thing every couple of years, but that could actually be interwoven into the texture and fabric of a creative life?

How can I create an ongoing community in a way that actually sustains and continually generates, fertilizes my creative ecosystem rather than depleting it? Is that possible for me?

community bounded by shared questing

I think about the difference between real life personal friends versus creative friends and how personal friendships come from shared life circumstances, but creative friendship are bound by our shared practice, shared obsessions, shared dilemmas, and shared questing.

The people I create community with are generally interested in non-conventional ways of discovering their own paths, outside of the culturally prescribed archetypes of what it means to be an artist or to have a business or to be successful.

The nature of our questing, making a body of work that actually can sustain us in all forms of the word sustain. This means that the community is often grappling with very similar questions around our relationship to time or attention or visibility or fear or money and resources.

When I think about building a community based on shared questing and shared companionship, I envision a community that is all about walking together. There's this onward forward motion to it. And maybe we go in circles, maybe we spiral, that is the metaphor of a labyrinth, but the core premise is about discovering and sharing these discoveries with each other.

the four guiding values

The first season of labyrinth was a total experiment, but in the second season, I spent a little bit of time trying to articulate the guiding ethos and values for how I want to create and invite people to be a part of this community. I've articulated four guiding values.

The first is mutual witnessing. The second is caring for self as caring for a whole. The third is collective resourcing. And the fourth is creative companionship in process. Let's unpack each a little bit together.

mutual witnessing

I really like the word mutual witnessing because the only requirement for mutual witnessing is to see the other and seek to understand the other. And to allow oneself to be seen is a gift for the rest of us. It's the opposite of performing, it's the opposite of conforming. It's allowing yourself to be seen as you are to express your truths, your vulnerabilities, and in doing so, also holding the same space for other people.

I see witnessing oneself, holding oneself, and witnessing others as two sides of the same coin. Because to practice self-compassion with parts of ourselves that we feel embarrassed about, I think that same compassion can extend to others because we are in many ways connected and universal and the same.

Witnessing is about acknowledgement. It doesn't mean you have to agree or know exactly the other person's life experiences, but it is a process of giving attention. And attention is an expression of love. Mutual witnessing is about practicing seeing the other and allowing yourself to be seen, which of course is sometimes much harder than it sounds.

caring for self as caring for whole

The second value is caring for oneself as caring for the whole. This is to say that when we tend to ourselves, when we resource ourselves, we are taking care of the collective body. This is about practicing the power in personal responsibility, support the group by supporting ourselves. And in doing so, we can offer our challenging experiences to the communal space.

I think those shares are gifts at the same time to bring awareness to what it is that you're asking for from the communal space, especially if there are difficult raw feelings to offer it with the energy of, this is what it's bringing up for me and taking responsibility for those feelings without implicitly asking the group to fix it or solve the problem can ultimately create space where more resourcing from the collective can actually happen.

It's like before asking for help, we have to make sure that the bowl from which we are asking doesn't have a leak in it.

collective resourcing

The third guiding value is collective resourcing. This is the idea that in order to be nourished by a community space, you have to tend to it to be an active part of it. In the flow of reciprocity of giving and receiving, to think of a communal space as something we cultivate together, like a garden or an experiment.

I really like the metaphor of a community garden because it's like we each have our own little plot, little container that we're growing something in. And we have the communal space where we grow together, where the flowers or plants cross-pollinate and fertilize each other. And during the harvest, we can share the bounty.

I also really like the phrase pooling our collective resources. It's like we each come to a communal space with decades of life experience and emotions and perspectives. And when we pool our resources together, we're putting everything into this giant pool that everyone can swim in.

Or I think about the feeling of sitting around a campfire at night, being warmed by the fire and the glow and offering things to the fire.

In collective resourcing, there's so many ways to give to the community. I think the practice of witnessing the other, seeing the other, of responding to other people is a deep way of giving. And allowing yourself to be seen in sharing something, an idea, a process, a system, an inspiration, or asking a question of the collective.

Sometimes it feels scary to allow ourselves to feel exposed and vulnerable. The act of giving activates the fear of being seen. Whereas for others, and including myself, sometimes the act of receiving can feel challenging, whether that's receiving attention or a compliment. In the practice of collective resourcing, it doesn't mean that what we give and receive has to be equal, but it does mean keeping the cycle in flow.

creative companionship in process

The fourth guiding value is creative companionship in process. I've been thinking a lot about the word companionship. To a younger version of me, it used to sound kind of boring, like it was less exciting than friendship and less exciting than romance. But these days I really like this word because companionship is about being together in the daily little things that make up an entire life.

In context of our family or friends that are companions, it's cooking together, going to bed, waking up, morning rituals, going on walks, doing laundry. In the case of creative companions, which is the theme of season two of "Labyrinth," it is about building the daily textures, weaving the web thread by thread, creating rituals, doing experiments, being in conversation with our daily rhythms and energy fluctuations. It's being with the mundanity of it.

The simple day-to-day struggles, not performing or sharing a big thing that we've created, but grappling with process, asking questions about the practice of rest or making time for creative work or celebrating the tiny incremental changes that are barely perceptible to other people. Maybe you felt differently when you shared something this time. Maybe looking at your money brought up less anxiety than it did before. Companionship is about noticing and paying attention to the small changes and that having significance.

We are companions in the process. We're discovering something together. We're embarking on quests together, sharing the encounters we have on those creative quests. The little moments of fear, resistance, flow, joy, fulfillment, that is the substance of the work.

community as dreamcatcher

When I think about these four values, I see mutual witnessing as the foundation of making space for each other and seeing each other, and then caring for self as caring for a whole as making sure that we are resourced on the ways in which we show up, collective resourcing as creating the community garden, giving and receiving from it, and creative companionship as the practice of daily walking.

So when we practice these four values or guiding principles, we can create a flexible, resilient ecosystem that will allow our individuality to be able to take up space and flourish while being connected, giving and receiving from the whole.

When I visualize this, I think about a circular form like a dream catcher, and all of these tiny threads intersecting across this circle. My role in holding the container is not to do all the work of holding all of the threads. I am not the central node, but I am holding the space for the circle.

This woven web has so much more resilience in being connected to each other. Very practically speaking, it makes me really happy to see people in the community supporting each other, connecting one-on-one, offering their insights and perspectives. I can zoom out and look at the community as a dream catcher web, and know that it's able to catch something magical and fluid in the spaces between all of us.

I think sometimes in energetically unsustainable situations, the more we give to something doesn't necessarily mean that we will get more back, whether this is a job or a depleting relationship of any sort. But I'm thinking about reciprocity a bit differently here. In the case of a creative community, you give to it by witnessing others, supporting others, and at the same time, being absolutely present with your creative process and sharing your journey and questions and insights you're having.

My vision for a community is one in which everyone is deeply invested in tending to their own work as a way of inspiring and offering companionship to all of us in our spiraling paths.

the long view

For me, I'm asking myself the question of, can I build a community that sustains and is generative over a long period of time?

I know that holding space for community is such a growth challenge for me because I've operated for so long as a lonely node in the void. To be in a position where people come seeking guidance and support and connection, it has encouraged me to stay centered in myself, to be aware of not overmanaging people's feelings, and to let it be something that can feel sustainable over time.

The old stories that I have been shedding are that community is at odds with pursuing my creative visions, that a community would restrict me or limit me or burden me, which is why I've always created a bit of distance, but I feel deeply that I am called to create community because there is deep potential for healing through cultivating belonging to ourselves in the relationships we build with others, the chosen bonds that we form through shared obsessions, shared passion, shared questing.

I am learning alongside Labyrinth how to hold space for a community in such a way that it can also hold me.

And so in thinking through season two of Labyrinth, the question that I had for myself is, how can Labyrinth be not a separate thing that I do, like teaching a course, but more integrated with the textures of my day-to-day creative life?

And through this question, I have decided to restructure Labyrinth into two parts. The Labyrinth is about the practice of communal walking, navigating our processes and creative work through live discussion sessions, creative tracks, show and tells, through collective resources or collaborations.

And then the second part is the Library, which is my collection of teachings and workshops and resources, and an experimental section will all share notes from my real-time messy processing, my work in progress, my journals, my notion systems. So as close as possible to my private world, it's like for the longest time I have my website world as the digital ecosystem, and then I had everything else, stacks and stacks of journals and notion pages and notes. And I've been thinking of my community space, Labyrinth, as the long corridor between public and private.

Rather than extracting from my private collections and private notes, I've been experiencing it as making my world even more multi-layered, allowing myself to explode even more in creativity and expand. And I'm discovering that the more I expand and grow and allow myself to be seen, the richer I feel, the more I feel free to offer my full cell to take up space.

One way of holding the community is doing what I do best, which is deep devotion to my personal processes and letting that be seen.

As I think about the shape of a community, I keep asking myself the question of, how can this space feel alive, generative, vibrant, something that is not at odds with my personal work, but which only enriches and deepens it and makes it more complex and more beautiful over time?

How can I encourage the members of Labyrinth to tend to that connection between the deeply personal and the shared collective abundance? I often describe it as a infinite feast. We all bring our own homemade dishes to the table. And sometimes we go away and sometimes we come back again. Sometimes we share meals together. Sometimes we snack alone at midnight, but there's a sense of always feeding ourselves and feeding each other.

I'm not just thinking about Labyrinth this year or next year, but imagining how it could be in five years or 10 years or 20, how will it accompany me over my life changes? How will it change? And I don't know yet.

I think that's part of the fun and excitement that having a business, creating a community container, creating any container really is about shaping and reshaping it an intimate living connection with the rest of our lives.

closing

So creative friends, if you'd like to join the next season of Labyrinth opens on Monday, I would be very happy to walk alongside you.

Thank you for listening. If you're interested in re-imagining business containers with me, I will be teaching a live course, Digital Abundance, starting in early March. The best way to keep in touch with my work is through my newsletter. You can explore more on my website world, different classes I'm teaching, or working together one-on-one.

Take care, until soon.
